cards.b: Header (destination address, packet number, originator's address), payload (the data) and trailer (marks the end, may hold error checking).
Message split into packets that travel independently by different routes, chosen by routers, and are reassembled in order at the destination.
Packets can arrive out of order, so the receiver uses the packet numbers to put them back in the right order.
Bits sent one at a time down a single wire. Reliable over long distances. Used by USB.
Several bits sent at once down several wires. Faster only over short distances; skewing and crosstalk cause errors over distance.
Simplex: one direction only. Half-duplex: both directions, not at the same time. Full-duplex: both directions at the same time.
Standard connector; devices detected automatically; can supply power; backward compatible; built-in error checking.
One extra bit makes the number of 1s in each byte even (even parity) or odd (odd parity). Detects errors but cannot say which bit is wrong.
If two bits change, the parity still looks correct, so the error is not detected.
A value calculated from the data by an algorithm and sent with it. The receiver recalculates and compares.
The receiver sends the data back to the sender, who compares it with the original. Differences show an error, but not where it happened.
Last digit of a code, calculated from the other digits. Catches data entry errors such as wrong or transposed digits.
Receiver sends a positive or negative acknowledgement. If negative, or no reply before the timeout, the sender resends the data.
Plaintext is the original data. Ciphertext is the scrambled result after encryption with a key.
Symmetric uses one shared key. Asymmetric uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt.

gaps.s: The actual data in a packet is called the ___.
Sending bits one at a time down a single wire is called ___ transmission.
Data sent in both directions at the same time is called ___ duplex.
In ARQ, the sender resends data if no acknowledgement arrives before the ___ expires.
A ___ digit is added to the end of a barcode number to detect data entry errors.
Scrambled data that cannot be understood is called ___.
Asymmetric encryption uses a public key and a ___ key.
The extra bit added to a byte so the number of 1s is even or odd is the ___ bit.

short.q: A byte is received using odd parity: 01101011. Has an error been detected? Explain.
short.model: 01101011 has five 1s, which is odd. Odd parity is expected, so no error is detected (though two changed bits would not be noticed).
points: odd matches odd parity so no error detected

short.q: Explain why packets of one message might arrive in a different order.
short.model: Each packet travels independently and may take a different route, chosen by routers, so some arrive sooner than others.

short.q: Give two reasons why serial transmission is used for long distances instead of parallel.
short.model: In parallel the bits can arrive out of sync (skew) and the wires interfere with each other (crosstalk), causing errors. Serial avoids this and the cable is cheaper.
points: parallel suffers skewing / bits arrive out of sync
crosstalk / interference, or serial cable cheaper

short.q: Describe how ARQ ensures data is received correctly.
short.model: The receiver checks the data and sends a positive acknowledgement if correct, or a negative one if not. The sender resends on a negative acknowledgement or if the timeout expires with no reply.
points: negative acknowledgement or timeout leads to resend

short.q: Explain one advantage of asymmetric encryption over symmetric encryption.
short.model: Asymmetric encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt, so the private key is never sent and cannot be intercepted. With symmetric encryption the shared key must be sent to the receiver.
points: public key encrypts, private key decrypts
the decryption key is never sent / symmetric key can be intercepted
